newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South African truth commission seen as skewed.
newsitem.headline: South African truth commission seen as skewed.

text.p: South Africa's opposition National Party is crying foul at alleged bias by Archbishop Desmond Tutu's truth commission, and independent political analysts agree the party has a point.

"The manner in which the cross-examination of NP leader F.W. de Klerk was handled is further evidence...of the lack of evenhandedness of elements in the Truth and Reconciliation Commission," the party said in a statement.
It was commenting on aggressive grilling of de Klerk at a hearing on Wednesday during which the commission probed the party's record on human rights abuses during apartheid.

Earlier in the week, President Nelson Mandela's African National Congress faced relatively gentle questioning over its role in fighting apartheid and its involvement in political violence with the rival black Inkatha Freedom Party.
"(The commission) dealt with Deputy President Thabo Mbeki at the ANC hearing in a comradely manner and in quite a jolly atmosphere," the National Party said.

Many South Africans would say the National Party deserved all it got from the commission, which suggested to de Klerk that his party presided over "state-sanctioned criminality" in its attempts to quash opposition to apartheid.
But political analyst Laurie Nathan said the commission should make a greater effort to be impartial.
"The commission has disclosed bias. Its commissioners have made clear that they do not regard the crimes of the ANC and the crimes of the NP in the same category," Nathan said.
"Now, I think they're correct. But I think it's inappropriate for a body which is intended to be objective, to make that assertion up front...
"I don't think you can compare the crime of apartheid with whatever crimes were committed in opposing apartheid, but I don't think the commission should be saying that out loud," he said.

David Welsh, political scientist at the University of Cape Town, said the commission's contrasting treatment of the two sides this week confirmed his belief that it was a political instrument rather than a body aimed at achieving genuine reconciliation.
"The ANC got off lightly... its evidence was not put under the microscope," Welsh said.
"The commission is a political instrument aimed at knocking (Inkatha leader) Mangosuthu Buthelezi and de Klerk off their perches.
"As far as reconciliation is concerned, well that's just gallows humour," he said.
Welsh said the ANC's assertion to the commission that it had never regarded Inkatha as a military opponent "stretched credibility".

About 15,000 people were killed in a decade of violence starting in the mid-1980s which according to conventional wisdom pitted the ANC against Inkatha in a fight for black support, particularly in KwaZulu-Natal province.
But in its submission this week the ANC denied ever casting the first stone at any stage of the violence, saying the battle was really between itself and agents of the white government.
Buthelezi issued a statement on Wednesday scoffing at this version. He said the ANC had killed at least 420 Inkatha leaders and thousands of ordinary Inkatha supporters.
In some respects, the testimony of Mbeki and de Klerk to the commission was remarkably similar.

Both acknowledged that their followers might have committed abuses or atrocities, but both said that in doing so the lower ranks acted on their own initiative and not in accordance with directives from above.
Nathan said the commission had succeeded in uncovering the truth about many of the crimes and human rights abuses committed during apartheid, but was likely to fail in achieving reconciliation.
"We know a hell of a lot more than we did previously... (but) I don't think reconciliation was ever possible through the truth commission," he said.
